{{short description|American mathematician}}[[File:Calkin-john w.jpg|thumb|Photo from Calkin's identification badge at Los Alamos.]]

'''John Williams Calkin'''<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://www.ams.org/notices/199702/comm-maclane.pdf|author=Mac Lane, Saunders|authorlink=Saunders Mac Lane|title=Requiem for the Skillful|journal=Notices of the AMS|volume=44|issue=2|pages=207–208|date=February 1997}} Mac Lane mentions Jack Calkin as one of the few mathematicians working in the [[Manhattan Project]] in Los Alamos, with John von Neumann, [[Stanislaw Ulam]], C. J. Everett, and [[Paul Olum]].</ref> (11 October 1909, [[New Rochelle, New York]] – 5 August 1964, [[Westhampton, New York]]) was an American mathematician, specializing in [[functional analysis]]. The [[Calkin algebra]] is named after him.<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.2307/1968771|jstor=1968771|title=Two-sided ideals and congruences in the ring of bounded operators in Hilbert space|journal=[[Annals of Mathematics]]|volume=42|issue=4|pages=839–873|year=1941|last1=Calkin|first1=John W.}}</ref>

==Biography==
Calkin received his bachelor's degree from [[Columbia University]] in 1933 and his master's degree in 1934 and his Ph.D. in 1937 from [[Harvard University]]. His doctoral dissertation '' Applications of the Theory of Hilbert Space to Partial Differential Equations; the Self-Adjoint Transformations in Hilbert Space Associated with a Formal Partial Differential Operator of the Second Order and Elliptic Type '') was supervised by [[Marshall H. Stone]]. In the dissertation, Calkin acknowledges useful discussions with [[John von Neumann]].<ref name=Hassi>{{cite book|last1=Hassi|first1=Seppo|title=Operator Methods for Boundary Value Problems|last2=de Snoo|first2=Hendrik S. V.|last3=Szafraniec|first3=Franciszek Hugon|chapter=John Williams Calkin: a short biography|year=2012|pages=1–2|doi=10.1017/CBO9781139135061.002|isbn=9781139135061}}</ref> At the [[Institute for Advanced Study]], Calkin was a research assistant for the academic year 1937–1938 (working with [[Oswald Veblen]] and von Neumann) and in the first eight months of 1942.<ref>{{cite web|title=John W. Calkin|website=Institute for Advanced Study|date=9 December 2019 |url=https://www.ias.edu/scholars/john-w-calkin}}</ref><ref name=Hassi/> From 1938 to 1942 he was an assistant professor at the [[University of New Hampshire]] and then at Chicago's [[Illinois Institute of Technology]]. During the late 1930s and early 1940s he wrote several important papers on operator theory and its applications to partial differential equations.<ref name=PhysicsToday>{{cite journal|doi=10.1063/1.3051213|title=John W. Calkin|journal=Physics Today|volume=17|issue=11|pages=102–105|year=1964|doi-access=free}}</ref>

{{blockquote|During World War II Calkin was part of a mine warfare operations analysis group with [[Joseph L. Doob|J.L. Doob]], J. von Neumann, and [[Marshall Harvey Stone|M.H. Stone]]. Von Neumann and Calkin worked on shock waves and damage by explosives; they were sent to England to learn of the progress under way there. When it appeared that their special knowledge would be useful for the [[Manhattan Project]], they moved to Los Alamos.<ref name=Hassi/>}}

From Los Alamos, Calkin went in 1946 as a [[Guggenheim Fellow]]<ref>{{cite web|title=John W. Calkin|website=John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation|url=https://www.gf.org/fellows/all-fellows/john-w-calkin/}}</ref> to the [[California Institute of Technology]]. He later taught at the [[Rice University|Rice Institute]] (renamed Rice University in 1960), before returning in 1949 to [[Los Alamos Scientific Laboratory]] as a member of the theoretical division.<ref name=PhysicsToday/> There he worked on the development of the H-bomb.

{{blockquote|In 1958, he accepted a consulting appointment at New York University and at Brookhaven National Laboratory and, in 1961, was named head, and then chairman of the Applied Mathematics Department.<ref name=PhysicsToday/>}}

Upon his death he was survived by his widow, Emilienne Calkin (1922–2000), and his son, Brant Calkin (born 1934), from a previous marriage (to Eileen Calkin).<ref>{{cite news|title=John W. Calkin, A Mathematician; Brookhaven Official Dead—Was at Los Alamos|date=6 August 1964|newspaper=NY Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1964/08/06/archives/john-w-calkin-a-mathematician-brookhaven-official-deadwas-at-los.html}}</ref> Brant Calkin is an environmental activist in New Mexico and Utah and a former president of the [[Sierra Club]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.canyoncountryzephyr.com/oldzephyr/archives/brant-calkin.html|title=Brant Calkin|author=Groene, Scott|website=canyoncountryzephyr.com}}</ref>
